title: Unconventional magnon-mediated spin torque enabled by ferroelectric domain engineering in multiferroic BiFeO_3

paper_content.abstract: Spin current provides an energy-efficient approach for manipulating magnetization, when its spin polarization aligns with the magnetization direction. However, conventional spin-source materials possess high crystalline symmetry, restricting spin polarization to be orthogonal to both spin and charge current directions. Here, we overcome this limitation by utilizing the concept of magnon-mediated spin-orbit torque through integration of the insulating multiferroic BiFeO with a conventional spin-source material. We observe that spin polarization generated by conventional spin-source material can excite unconventional magnon polarization due to the interplay between cycloidal antiferromagnetic order and the ferroelectric domain structure in BiFeO . This produces an unconventional magnon torque that allows deterministic, field‑free switching of in‑plane magnetization collinear with the current direction, unattainable with conventional spin-source materials. Our results establish multiferroic-based heterostructure as a symmetry‑engineered magnon spin source, paving the way for low-power spintronic devices.
paper_content.introduction:
Spin currents, flows of spin angular momentum characterized by their spin polarization (𝝈 enable efficiently manipulating magnetization via spin-orbit torques1, crucial for developing emerging magnetic logic and memory devices2-6. Electron-mediated spin currents can be induced by the spin Hall effect7,8 (SHE or Rashba-Edelstein effect9 (REE in spin-source materials. Nevertheless, the most commonly used spin-source materials, such as polycrystalline heavy metals10, exhibit high crystalline symmetry, constraining spin polarization 𝛔 to be orthogonal to both the charge and spin current directions. Specifically, when a charge current (𝐽 flowing along the x-axis generates a spin current (𝐽 propagating along the z-axis, the spin polarization is confined strictly to the y-axis, producing only a conventional damping-like spin torque 𝛕 𝑦 ∝ 𝐌×(𝐲×𝐌) (Fig. 1a . As a result, efficient field-free magnetization switching is limited exclusively to the y-axis11. Achieving efficient field-free switching along other axes, which is desirable for low-power, high density magnetic devices, requires unconventional spin polarization (with 𝛔 deviating from the y-axis 2. Such unconventional spin polarizations have been observed in spin-source materials with reduced crystalline symmetry (Fig. 1b 12-16, or materials with non-collinear antiferromagnetic17-21 or altermagnetic orders22-24.

Alternatively, spin angular momentum can be carried by magnons, the collective excitations of magnetic orders, which efficiently propagate magnon currents (𝐽 through magnetically-ordered insulators over long distances without involving charge transport25-32. In heterostructures of spin-source/antiferromagnetic-insulator/ferromagnet, spin currents from a spin-source layer excite magnons in the antiferromagnetic insulator, generating a magnon current that subsequently exerts magnon torque on an adjacent ferromagnetic layer33-35. This approach presents an attractive pathway toward more energy-efficient spintronic devices36. More importantly, this magnon-mediated spin torque can leverage the symmetry of the antiferromagnetic layer, offering an additional degree of freedom for spin torque engineering. Recent studies have shown that the amplitude of magnon torque can be tuned by controlling the ferroelectric order in heterostructure incorporating multiferroic BiFeO 37-39. However, controlling the magnon spin polarization direction to generate unconventional magnon torques remains unexplored.

In this work, we experimentally demonstrate that two-variant ferroelectric domains with distinct spin cycloid structure in BiFeO enable control over magnon spin polarization (Fig. 1c . In epitaxial SrRuO /BiFeO /Ni Fe heterostructures, we observe efficient generation of unconventional magnon torque 𝛕𝑥 ∝𝐌×(𝐱×𝐌), with spin polarization rotated by up to 11° from the conventional y-axis direction dictated by symmetry. This unconventional magnon torque strongly depends on the orientation of the ferroelectric domains and is absent in samples with disordered domains, consistent with symmetry analysis of BiFeO possessing ferroelectrically coupled spin cycloid structures. We further demonstrate deterministic, field-free magnetization switching along the x-axis which is prohibited by symmetry with conventional spin torque. These results reveal that control of the ferroelectric domain structures in multiferroic materials provide a route to leverage hidden symmetries within the antiferromagnetic order, opening pathways for advanced functionalities in future magnon-based spintronic devices.

Symmetry analysis of BiFeO with spin cycloid structure
Bulk BiFeO possesses a pseudocubic perovskite lattice with a slight rhombohedral distortion40. The breaking of inversion symmetry in BiFeO induces robust ferroelectric polarization 𝐏41 (approximately 100 μC/cm2 oriented along one of the eight possible pseudocubic [111] directions, forming eight ferroelectric variants (𝐏± , as illustrated in Fig. 2a. These eight ferroelectric variants give rise to three possible types of ferroelectric domain walls (71°, 109° and 180° 42. The inversion symmetry breaking also leads to a strong Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM interaction characterized by a pseudovector 𝐃 that is perpendicular to 𝐏37. For instance, when 𝐏 points along [111], 𝐃 oriented along [112̅ ] cants the antiferromagnetically coupled Fe3+ magnetic moments, leading to a spin cycloid structure that couples strongly to the magnon band structure and magnon transport43-46. Another intrinsic DM interaction parallel to 𝐏 accounts for non-compensation of the magnetic moments in BiFeO , though this contribution is relatively small47,48. Therefore, the chirality of the Fe3+ spin cycloid is predominantly determined by 𝐃. We exploit the symmetries of the cycloidal spin structure to control magnon-mediated spin currents by engineering the ferroelectric domain structure in BiFeO . In two-variant domain BiFeO that can be stabilized through strain50 or substrate vicinality51, the cycloidal propagation vector 𝐤 is constrained within the sample plane and remains orthogonal to 𝐏50,52. Deterministic, field-free type-x magnetization switching
Finally, we demonstrate that this unconventional magnon torque 𝛕𝑥 can drive deterministic field-free switching of magnetization along the x-axis (referred to as type-x switching , as schematically shown in Fig. 4a. To understand the role of 𝛕𝑥 in switching dynamics, we performed macro-spin simulations for field-free type-x switching, incorporating a damping-like magnon torque with an in-plane spin polarization canted by 11°, consistent with that observed in our sample (see Methods . Figure 4b shows the simulated trajectories of magnetization with initial magnetization along +x direction. paper_content.methods:
Sample growth
Epitaxial SrRuO /BiFeO heterostructures were deposited on (110 -oriented DyScO substrates using pulsed laser deposition (PLD with a 248 nm KrF excimer laser. SrRuO and BiFeO were deposited at substrate temperature of 670 ℃ and 700 °C, under an oxygen partial pressure of 110 mTorr and 150 mTorr, respectively. The laser fluence at the target surfaces was approximately 1.5 J/cm2 with a pulse repetition rate of 5-7 Hz. Subsequently, the samples were cooled to room temperature in an oxygen rich atmosphere and transferred through air to a magnetron sputtering chamber with a base pressure of 1×10-8 Torr for the deposition of ferromagnetic metals. The ferromagnetic Ni Fe layer was deposited at an argon pressure of 3 mTorr, followed by the deposition of a 3 nm Ti capping layer to prevent oxidation. Film thicknesses were measured using X-ray reflectivity.

Device fabrication
Devices for ST-FMR and second harmonic Hall measurements were fabricated on the same sample chip using standard photolithography, followed by argon ion milling. Subsequently, 10 nm Ti / 150 nm Cu bilayers were deposited for electrode contacts using standard lift-off process. ST-FMR devices were patterned into 16 μm-wide and 80 μm-long microstrips with ground-signal-ground (GSG electrodes, while devices for second harmonic Hall measurements were patterned into 16 μm-wide and 80 μm-long Hall bars with 4 μm-wide Hall contacts.

Magnon torque measurements
For ST-FMR measurements, a Keysight E8257D microwave generator was used to provide a 15 dBm microwave excitation, modulated by an internal oscillator at 1713 Hz. The mixing voltage signal was detected using a DSP 7265 lock-in amplifier. For second harmonic Hall measurements, an AC current at 2333 Hz was supplied by the internal voltage source of the DSP 7265 lock-in amplifier. Both the first and second harmonic Hall voltage signals were simultaneously recorded using a single DSP 7265. Magnetic fields for both ST-FMR and second harmonic Hall measurements were applied using a GMLW projected-field magnet mounted on a Newport motion-controlled stage.

Magnon-torque-induced magnetization switching measurements
Field-free magnetization switching induced by magnon torque was measured using a probe station under zero applied magnetic field. Magnetization switching assisted by an out-of-plane magnetic field, as described in Supplementary Note 9, was performed in a Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS). All measurements were conducted at room temperature. A Keithley 6221 source meter was used to generate a single square wave with a 1 ms period and a 50% duty cycle, corresponding to a pulse duration of 500 μs. Following the application of the current pulse, the system waited for 8 s before measuring the second harmonic Hall voltage using a DSP 7265 lock-in amplifier at a frequency of 2333 Hz and a current amplitude of 2 mA.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Liang et al. report an unconventional magnon-mediated spin torque in BiFeO3-based heterostructures with a two-variant ferroelectric domain structure. The authors demonstrate that reduced symmetry permits an unconventional spin polarization collinear with the applied charge current, enabling deterministic, field-free switching of magnetization.
Magnon transport in multiferroics is of considerable interest nowadays because the magnon torque can be tuned by controlling the ferroelectric order. In addition, symmetry-breaking routes to unconventional spin polarization and associated field-free spin-orbit-torque switching are currently central topics in spin-orbitronics. By combining ferroelectric-order-dependent symmetry breaking with magnon torque to realize field-free switching, this work is both important and timely. We support publication of this manuscript in Nature Communications after the authors have considered the following minor comments:
1. While discussed elsewhere, a concise in-paper explanation of the microscopic mechanism for the unconventional spin polarization $\sigma_x$ would greatly help readers.
2. What is the role of having “TWO” ferroelectric domains? Is the TWO-variant state essential for the observed effect or is a single-domain state with an appropriate orientation sufficient?
3. In line 108,’ $D_1$ along $[\overline{1}\ 1\ 2]$’ seems to be a typo. It should read ‘$D_1$ along $[\overline{1}\ 1\ \overline{2}]$’.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript presents a highly significant and compelling study on the generation of an unconventional magnon-mediated spin torque in SrRuO₃/BiFeO₃/Ni₈₀Fe₂₀ heterostructures. The authors expertly leverage ferroelectric domain engineering in the multiferroic insulator BiFeO₃ to break the crystalline symmetry constraints that typically limit spin polarization in conventional spin-source materials. The experimental demonstration of a magnon torque with a spin polarization rotated by ~11° from the conventional y-axis, enabled by the specific spin cycloid structures in BiFeO₃, is a notable achievement. Furthermore, the subsequent demonstration of deterministic, field-free magnetization switching along the current direction (type-x switching) provides a crucial proof-of-concept for advanced, low-power spintronic devices. The work is meticulously executed, combining sophisticated symmetry analysis, thorough spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) measurements, and convincing switching experiments. The potential impact of this work on the fields of magnonics and spintronics is substantial. While the work is compelling and of high value, its impact could be further strengthened by addressing the following aspects:
1. While the authors provide a superb symmetry analysis proving that an in-plane unconventional torque is allowed, the manuscript lacks a detailed discussion on the specific microscopic mechanism that generates this non-y polarization. How exactly does the interaction between the spin current from SrRuO₃ and the unique spin cycloid in BiFeO₃ lead to a magnon current with a tilted spin polarization? A deeper physical explanation, potentially discussing the role of the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya vector, the coupling efficiency to different magnon modes, or the spin-to-magnon conversion process at the interface, would greatly enhance the fundamental understanding and impact of this work.
2. The experiments are conducted at room temperature, which is above the Curie temperature of SrRuO₃ (~160 K). The authors should include a brief discussion or citation to justify that SrRuO₃ retains sufficient spin-Hall conductivity in its paramagnetic state at 300 K to generate the observed effects.
3. A critical observation from Figures 3f and 3g is that the measurement uncertainties (error bars) for the unconventional torque efficiency appear to be an order of magnitude smaller than those for the conventional torque efficiency . Given that both are extracted from fitting the same set of ST-FMR curves, this significant discrepancy requires a clear explanation. The precise measurement of the torque efficiency is the direct experimental proof of the unconventional torque, and such a large difference in uncertainty could raise questions about the fitting procedure or the robustness of the signal. Is this due to a higher signal-to-noise ratio for the sinφHsin2φH angular dependence? Or does it stem from the fitting model itself, where the conventional torque component is more susceptible to confounding factors (e.g., Oersted fields, variations in anisotropy)? A discussion on the origin of these error bars and the reasons for their disparity is essential to firmly establish the credibility of the central finding.
4. The work on field-free switching is impressive. However, the explanation of the switching mechanism could be further strengthened to clarify the specific roles of the different polarization components. It is necessary for the authors to provide a clearer explanation, either in the theoretical analysis or discussion section, regarding the relative contributions and influence of the y-polarization and x-polarization components in driving the field-free switching process. In addition, the authors effectively contrast the switching behavior at φE = 30° and φE = 90° to demonstrate the deterministic role of the x-polarization component. To further solidify this claim, a complementary experimental data point at φE = 135° would be highly informative. Would the switching polarity be expected to reverse at this angle? Including this result could serve as another direct and compelling evidence for the existence and critical role of the x-polarization component.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
Liang et al. reported the observation of unconventional magnon torque in SrRuO3/BiFeO3/NiFe heterostructures, where the unconventional magnon spin polarization is governed by the ferroelectric domain structure of multiferroic BiFeO3. The authors analyzed the symmetry of the two-variant ferroelectric domain structure and demonstrated that the ferroelectric domains can break magnetic mirror symmetry for unconventional torque. They then fabricated devices with controlled ferroelectric domains and observed the in-plane unconventional magnon torque through STFMR and harmonic measurements, and further demonstrated field-free type-x magnetization switching. The underlying physics is interesting and the topic is timely, supported by convincing results.
I would recommend publication of this manuscript in Nature Communications if the authors address the following points:
1. Could the authors provide additional symmetry analyses for other possible ferroelectric domain structures, such as the single-domain and four-variant domain configurations that are commonly observed in BiFeO3 thin films? Including these cases would help readers better understand and generalize the presented results.
2. According to the symmetry analysis, only one mirror plane exists in the two-variant domain structure, why only sigma_x is observed?
3. Can the authors exclude the interfacial origin of the unconventional torque?
4. Will field-like torque affect the switching?
5. There are some typos that authors should check, for example in Supplementary Fig. 8c the y-axis label is wrong.

## Abstract

Spin current provides an energy-efficient approach for manipulating magnetization, when its spin polarization aligns with the magnetization direction. However, conventional spin-source materials possess high crystalline symmetry, restricting spin polarization to be orthogonal to both spin and charge current directions. Here, we overcome this limitation by utilizing the concept of magnon-mediated spin-orbit torque through integration of the insulating multiferroic BiFeO with a conventional spin-source material. We observe that spin polarization generated by conventional spin-source material can excite unconventional magnon polarization due to the interplay between cycloidal antiferromagnetic order and the ferroelectric domain structure in BiFeO . This produces an unconventional magnon torque that allows deterministic, field‑free switching of in‑plane magnetization collinear with the current direction, unattainable with conventional spin-source materials. Our results establish multiferroic-based heterostructure as a symmetry‑engineered magnon spin source, paving the way for low-power spintronic devices.

## Introduction

Spin currents, flows of spin angular momentum characterized by their spin polarization (𝝈 enable efficiently manipulating magnetization via spin-orbit torques1, crucial for developing emerging magnetic logic and memory devices2-6. Electron-mediated spin currents can be induced by the spin Hall effect7,8 (SHE or Rashba-Edelstein effect9 (REE in spin-source materials. Nevertheless, the most commonly used spin-source materials, such as polycrystalline heavy metals10, exhibit high crystalline symmetry, constraining spin polarization 𝛔 to be orthogonal to both the charge and spin current directions. Specifically, when a charge current (𝐽 flowing along the x-axis generates a spin current (𝐽 propagating along the z-axis, the spin polarization is confined strictly to the y-axis, producing only a conventional damping-like spin torque 𝛕 𝑦 ∝ 𝐌×(𝐲×𝐌) (Fig. 1a . As a result, efficient field-free magnetization switching is limited exclusively to the y-axis11. Achieving efficient field-free switching along other axes, which is desirable for low-power, high density magnetic devices, requires unconventional spin polarization (with 𝛔 deviating from the y-axis 2. Such unconventional spin polarizations have been observed in spin-source materials with reduced crystalline symmetry (Fig. 1b 12-16, or materials with non-collinear antiferromagnetic17-21 or altermagnetic orders22-24.

Alternatively, spin angular momentum can be carried by magnons, the collective excitations of magnetic orders, which efficiently propagate magnon currents (𝐽 through magnetically-ordered insulators over long distances without involving charge transport25-32. In heterostructures of spin-source/antiferromagnetic-insulator/ferromagnet, spin currents from a spin-source layer excite magnons in the antiferromagnetic insulator, generating a magnon current that subsequently exerts magnon torque on an adjacent ferromagnetic layer33-35. This approach presents an attractive pathway toward more energy-efficient spintronic devices36. More importantly, this magnon-mediated spin torque can leverage the symmetry of the antiferromagnetic layer, offering an additional degree of freedom for spin torque engineering. Recent studies have shown that the amplitude of magnon torque can be tuned by controlling the ferroelectric order in heterostructure incorporating multiferroic BiFeO 37-39. However, controlling the magnon spin polarization direction to generate unconventional magnon torques remains unexplored.

Spin current provides an energy-efficient approach for manipulating magnetization, when its spin polarization aligns with the magnetization direction. However, conventional spin-source materials possess high crystalline symmetry, restricting spin polarization to be orthogonal to both spin and charge current directions. Here, we overcome this limitation by utilizing the concept of magnon-mediated spin-orbit torque through integration of the insulating multiferroic BiFeO with a conventional spin-source material. ## Introduction

Spin currents, flows of spin angular momentum characterized by their spin polarization (𝝈 enable efficiently manipulating magnetization via spin-orbit torques1, crucial for developing emerging magnetic logic and memory devices2-6. Electron-mediated spin currents can be induced by the spin Hall effect7,8 (SHE or Rashba-Edelstein effect9 (REE in spin-source materials. Nevertheless, the most commonly used spin-source materials, such as polycrystalline heavy metals10, exhibit high crystalline symmetry, constraining spin polarization 𝛔 to be orthogonal to both the charge and spin current directions. Specifically, when a charge current (𝐽 flowing along the x-axis generates a spin current (𝐽 propagating along the z-axis, the spin polarization is confined strictly to the y-axis, producing only a conventional damping-like spin torque 𝛕 𝑦 ∝ 𝐌×(𝐲×𝐌) (Fig. 1a . As a result, efficient field-free magnetization switching is limited exclusively to the y-axis11. Achieving efficient field-free switching along other axes, which is desirable for low-power, high density magnetic devices, requires unconventional spin polarization (with 𝛔 deviating from the y-axis 2. Such unconventional spin polarizations have been observed in spin-source materials with reduced crystalline symmetry (Fig. 1b 12-16, or materials with non-collinear antiferromagnetic17-21 or altermagnetic orders22-24.

This approach presents an attractive pathway toward more energy-efficient spintronic devices36. More importantly, this magnon-mediated spin torque can leverage the symmetry of the antiferromagnetic layer, offering an additional degree of freedom for spin torque engineering. Recent studies have shown that the amplitude of magnon torque can be tuned by controlling the ferroelectric order in heterostructure incorporating multiferroic BiFeO 37-39. However, controlling the magnon spin polarization direction to generate unconventional magnon torques remains unexplored.

## Methods

Sample growth
Epitaxial SrRuO /BiFeO heterostructures were deposited on (110 -oriented DyScO substrates using pulsed laser deposition (PLD with a 248 nm KrF excimer laser. SrRuO and BiFeO were deposited at substrate temperature of 670 ℃ and 700 °C, under an oxygen partial pressure of 110 mTorr and 150 mTorr, respectively. The laser fluence at the target surfaces was approximately 1.5 J/cm2 with a pulse repetition rate of 5-7 Hz. Subsequently, the samples were cooled to room temperature in an oxygen rich atmosphere and transferred through air to a magnetron sputtering chamber with a base pressure of 1×10-8 Torr for the deposition of ferromagnetic metals. The ferromagnetic Ni Fe layer was deposited at an argon pressure of 3 mTorr, followed by the deposition of a 3 nm Ti capping layer to prevent oxidation. Film thicknesses were measured using X-ray reflectivity.

Device fabrication
Devices for ST-FMR and second harmonic Hall measurements were fabricated on the same sample chip using standard photolithography, followed by argon ion milling. Subsequently, 10 nm Ti / 150 nm Cu bilayers were deposited for electrode contacts using standard lift-off process. ST-FMR devices were patterned into 16 μm-wide and 80 μm-long microstrips with ground-signal-ground (GSG electrodes, while devices for second harmonic Hall measurements were patterned into 16 μm-wide and 80 μm-long Hall bars with 4 μm-wide Hall contacts.

Magnon torque measurements
For ST-FMR measurements, a Keysight E8257D microwave generator was used to provide a 15 dBm microwave excitation, modulated by an internal oscillator at 1713 Hz. The mixing voltage signal was detected using a DSP 7265 lock-in amplifier. For second harmonic Hall measurements, an AC current at 2333 Hz was supplied by the internal voltage source of the DSP 7265 lock-in amplifier. Both the first and second harmonic Hall voltage signals were simultaneously recorded using a single DSP 7265. Magnetic fields for both ST-FMR and second harmonic Hall measurements were applied using a GMLW projected-field magnet mounted on a Newport motion-controlled stage.

## Paper

## Abstract

Spin current provides an energy-efficient approach for manipulating magnetization, when its spin polarization aligns with the magnetization direction. However, conventional spin-source materials possess high crystalline symmetry, restricting spin polarization to be orthogonal to both spin and charge current directions. Here, we overcome this limitation by utilizing the concept of magnon-mediated spin-orbit torque through integration of the insulating multiferroic BiFeO with a conventional spin-source material. We observe that spin polarization generated by conventional spin-source material can excite unconventional magnon polarization due to the interplay between cycloidal antiferromagnetic order and the ferroelectric domain structure in BiFeO . This produces an unconventional magnon torque that allows deterministic, field‑free switching of in‑plane magnetization collinear with the current direction, unattainable with conventional spin-source materials. Our results establish multiferroic-based heterostructure as a symmetry‑engineered magnon spin source, paving the way for low-power spintronic devices.

## Introduction

Spin currents, flows of spin angular momentum characterized by their spin polarization (𝝈 enable efficiently manipulating magnetization via spin-orbit torques1, crucial for developing emerging magnetic logic and memory devices2-6. Electron-mediated spin currents can be induced by the spin Hall effect7,8 (SHE or Rashba-Edelstein effect9 (REE in spin-source materials. Nevertheless, the most commonly used spin-source materials, such as polycrystalline heavy metals10, exhibit high crystalline symmetry, constraining spin polarization 𝛔 to be orthogonal to both the charge and spin current directions. Specifically, when a charge current (𝐽 flowing along the x-axis generates a spin current (𝐽 propagating along the z-axis, the spin polarization is confined strictly to the y-axis, producing only a conventional damping-like spin torque 𝛕 𝑦 ∝ 𝐌×(𝐲×𝐌) (Fig. 1a . As a result, efficient field-free magnetization switching is limited exclusively to the y-axis11. Achieving efficient field-free switching along other axes, which is desirable for low-power, high density magnetic devices, requires unconventional spin polarization (with 𝛔 deviating from the y-axis 2. Such unconventional spin polarizations have been observed in spin-source materials with reduced crystalline symmetry (Fig. 1b 12-16, or materials with non-collinear antiferromagnetic17-21 or altermagnetic orders22-24.

Alternatively, spin angular momentum can be carried by magnons, the collective excitations of magnetic orders, which efficiently propagate magnon currents (𝐽 through magnetically-ordered insulators over long distances without involving charge transport25-32. In heterostructures of spin-source/antiferromagnetic-insulator/ferromagnet, spin currents from a spin-source layer excite magnons in the antiferromagnetic insulator, generating a magnon current that subsequently exerts magnon torque on an adjacent ferromagnetic layer33-35. This approach presents an attractive pathway toward more energy-efficient spintronic devices36. More importantly, this magnon-mediated spin torque can leverage the symmetry of the antiferromagnetic layer, offering an additional degree of freedom for spin torque engineering. Recent studies have shown that the amplitude of magnon torque can be tuned by controlling the ferroelectric order in heterostructure incorporating multiferroic BiFeO 37-39. However, controlling the magnon spin polarization direction to generate unconventional magnon torques remains unexplored.

In this work, we experimentally demonstrate that two-variant ferroelectric domains with distinct spin cycloid structure in BiFeO enable control over magnon spin polarization (Fig. 1c . In epitaxial SrRuO /BiFeO /Ni Fe heterostructures, we observe efficient generation of unconventional magnon torque 𝛕𝑥 ∝𝐌×(𝐱×𝐌), with spin polarization rotated by up to 11° from the conventional y-axis direction dictated by symmetry. This unconventional magnon torque strongly depends on the orientation of the ferroelectric domains and is absent in samples with disordered domains, consistent with symmetry analysis of BiFeO possessing ferroelectrically coupled spin cycloid structures. We further demonstrate deterministic, field-free magnetization switching along the x-axis which is prohibited by symmetry with conventional spin torque. These results reveal that control of the ferroelectric domain structures in multiferroic materials provide a route to leverage hidden symmetries within the antiferromagnetic order, opening pathways for advanced functionalities in future magnon-based spintronic devices.

Symmetry analysis of BiFeO with spin cycloid structure
Bulk BiFeO possesses a pseudocubic perovskite lattice with a slight rhombohedral distortion40. ## Methods

Sample growth
Epitaxial SrRuO /BiFeO heterostructures were deposited on (110 -oriented DyScO substrates using pulsed laser deposition (PLD with a 248 nm KrF excimer laser. SrRuO and BiFeO were deposited at substrate temperature of 670 ℃ and 700 °C, under an oxygen partial pressure of 110 mTorr and 150 mTorr, respectively. The laser fluence at the target surfaces was approximately 1.5 J/cm2 with a pulse repetition rate of 5-7 Hz. Subsequently, the samples were cooled to room temperature in an oxygen rich atmosphere and transferred through air to a magnetron sputtering chamber with a base pressure of 1×10-8 Torr for the deposition of ferromagnetic metals. The ferromagnetic Ni Fe layer was deposited at an argon pressure of 3 mTorr, followed by the deposition of a 3 nm Ti capping layer to prevent oxidation. Film thicknesses were measured using X-ray reflectivity.

Device fabrication
Devices for ST-FMR and second harmonic Hall measurements were fabricated on the same sample chip using standard photolithography, followed by argon ion milling. Subsequently, 10 nm Ti / 150 nm Cu bilayers were deposited for electrode contacts using standard lift-off process. ST-FMR devices were patterned into 16 μm-wide and 80 μm-long microstrips with ground-signal-ground (GSG electrodes, while devices for second harmonic Hall measurements were patterned into 16 μm-wide and 80 μm-long Hall bars with 4 μm-wide Hall contacts.

Magnon torque measurements
For ST-FMR measurements, a Keysight E8257D microwave generator was used to provide a 15 dBm microwave excitation, modulated by an internal oscillator at 1713 Hz. The mixing voltage signal was detected using a DSP 7265 lock-in amplifier. For second harmonic Hall measurements, an AC current at 2333 Hz was supplied by the internal voltage source of the DSP 7265 lock-in amplifier. Both the first and second harmonic Hall voltage signals were simultaneously recorded using a single DSP 7265. Magnetic fields for both ST-FMR and second harmonic Hall measurements were applied using a GMLW projected-field magnet mounted on a Newport motion-controlled stage.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Liang et al. report an unconventional magnon-mediated spin torque in BiFeO3-based heterostructures with a two-variant ferroelectric domain structure. The authors demonstrate that reduced symmetry permits an unconventional spin polarization collinear with the applied charge current, enabling deterministic, field-free switching of magnetization.
Magnon transport in multiferroics is of considerable interest nowadays because the magnon torque can be tuned by controlling the ferroelectric order. In addition, symmetry-breaking routes to unconventional spin polarization and associated field-free spin-orbit-torque switching are currently central topics in spin-orbitronics. By combining ferroelectric-order-dependent symmetry breaking with magnon torque to realize field-free switching, this work is both important and timely. We support publication of this manuscript in Nature Communications after the authors have considered the following minor comments:
1. While discussed elsewhere, a concise in-paper explanation of the microscopic mechanism for the unconventional spin polarization $\sigma_x$ would greatly help readers.
2. What is the role of having “TWO” ferroelectric domains? Is the TWO-variant state essential for the observed effect or is a single-domain state with an appropriate orientation sufficient?
3. In line 108,’ $D_1$ along $[\overline{1}\ 1\ 2]$’ seems to be a typo. It should read ‘$D_1$ along $[\overline{1}\ 1\ \overline{2}]$’.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents a highly significant and compelling study on the generation of an unconventional magnon-mediated spin torque in SrRuO₃/BiFeO₃/Ni₈₀Fe₂₀ heterostructures. The authors expertly leverage ferroelectric domain engineering in the multiferroic insulator BiFeO₃ to break the crystalline symmetry constraints that typically limit spin polarization in conventional spin-source materials. The experimental demonstration of a magnon torque with a spin polarization rotated by ~11° from the conventional y-axis, enabled by the specific spin cycloid structures in BiFeO₃, is a notable achievement. Furthermore, the subsequent demonstration of deterministic, field-free magnetization switching along the current direction (type-x switching) provides a crucial proof-of-concept for advanced, low-power spintronic devices. The work is meticulously executed, combining sophisticated symmetry analysis, thorough spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) measurements, and convincing switching experiments. The potential impact of this work on the fields of magnonics and spintronics is substantial. While the work is compelling and of high value, its impact could be further strengthened by addressing the following aspects:
1. While the authors provide a superb symmetry analysis proving that an in-plane unconventional torque is allowed, the manuscript lacks a detailed discussion on the specific microscopic mechanism that generates this non-y polarization. How exactly does the interaction between the spin current from SrRuO₃ and the unique spin cycloid in BiFeO₃ lead to a magnon current with a tilted spin polarization? A deeper physical explanation, potentially discussing the role of the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya vector, the coupling efficiency to different magnon modes, or the spin-to-magnon conversion process at the interface, would greatly enhance the fundamental understanding and impact of this work.
2. The experiments are conducted at room temperature, which is above the Curie temperature of SrRuO₃ (~160 K). The authors should include a brief discussion or citation to justify that SrRuO₃ retains sufficient spin-Hall conductivity in its paramagnetic state at 300 K to generate the observed effects.
3. A critical observation from Figures 3f and 3g is that the measurement uncertainties (error bars) for the unconventional torque efficiency appear to be an order of magnitude smaller than those for the conventional torque efficiency . Given that both are extracted from fitting the same set of ST-FMR curves, this significant discrepancy requires a clear explanation. The precise measurement of the torque efficiency is the direct experimental proof of the unconventional torque, and such a large difference in uncertainty could raise questions about the fitting procedure or the robustness of the signal. Is this due to a higher signal-to-noise ratio for the sinφHsin2φH angular dependence? Or does it stem from the fitting model itself, where the conventional torque component is more susceptible to confounding factors (e.g., Oersted fields, variations in anisotropy)? A discussion on the origin of these error bars and the reasons for their disparity is essential to firmly establish the credibility of the central finding.
4. The work on field-free switching is impressive. However, the explanation of the switching mechanism could be further strengthened to clarify the specific roles of the different polarization components. It is necessary for the authors to provide a clearer explanation, either in the theoretical analysis or discussion section, regarding the relative contributions and influence of the y-polarization and x-polarization components in driving the field-free switching process. In addition, the authors effectively contrast the switching behavior at φE = 30° and φE = 90° to demonstrate the deterministic role of the x-polarization component. To further solidify this claim, a complementary experimental data point at φE = 135° would be highly informative. Would the switching polarity be expected to reverse at this angle? Including this result could serve as another direct and compelling evidence for the existence and critical role of the x-polarization component.

### Reviewer 4

Liang et al. reported the observation of unconventional magnon torque in SrRuO3/BiFeO3/NiFe heterostructures, where the unconventional magnon spin polarization is governed by the ferroelectric domain structure of multiferroic BiFeO3. The authors analyzed the symmetry of the two-variant ferroelectric domain structure and demonstrated that the ferroelectric domains can break magnetic mirror symmetry for unconventional torque. They then fabricated devices with controlled ferroelectric domains and observed the in-plane unconventional magnon torque through STFMR and harmonic measurements, and further demonstrated field-free type-x magnetization switching. The underlying physics is interesting and the topic is timely, supported by convincing results.
I would recommend publication of this manuscript in Nature Communications if the authors address the following points:
1. Could the authors provide additional symmetry analyses for other possible ferroelectric domain structures, such as the single-domain and four-variant domain configurations that are commonly observed in BiFeO3 thin films? Including these cases would help readers better understand and generalize the presented results.
2. According to the symmetry analysis, only one mirror plane exists in the two-variant domain structure, why only sigma_x is observed?
3. Can the authors exclude the interfacial origin of the unconventional torque?
4. Will field-like torque affect the switching?
5. There are some typos that authors should check, for example in Supplementary Fig. 8c the y-axis label is wrong.
